anomalies.observed: U10 pin5 (GND2) and U11 pin5 (GND2) are connected to the main GND net. U10 pin8 (VCC2) and U11 pin8 (VCC2) are connected to 5V_switched_CAN, which is derived from the non-isolated +5V rail via Q9.
anomalies.expected: For isolated CAN transceivers, GND2 should be on an isolated ground and VCC2 on an isolated supply, separate from the logic-side GND and +5V.

evidence.quote: two isolated CAN buses (CAN0, CAN1), each driven by its own MCP2515 SPI CAN controller (U8, U9) through an isolated CAN transceiver (U11/companion)

anomalies.impact: Galvanic isolation is defeated; ground loops and common-mode voltages can damage transceivers or connected devices, and the board does not meet the intended isolated CAN interface.

anomalies.observed: D30 pin4 (A2) is on ESTOP_OUT. D30 pin2 (K2) connects to R60 pin1; R60 pin2 is also on ESTOP_OUT. Thus the second LED of D30 is connected between ESTOP_OUT and ESTOP_OUT through R60.
anomalies.expected: The e-stop status LED should be connected between ESTOP_OUT and GND (e.g., R60 to GND) so it can illuminate when ESTOP_OUT is active.
anomalies.impact: The e-stop LED will never light, removing visual indication of e-stop status.

anomalies.observed: U21 pin13 (3V3OUT) is connected to +3V3, the same net as U21 pin15 (VCC) and pin3 (VCCIO).
anomalies.expected: When the FT231XS is powered from 3.3V on VCC, the internal LDO output 3V3OUT should be left unconnected (or decoupled) and not tied to the 3.3V rail, to avoid back-driving the internal regulator.
anomalies.impact: Potential contention between the external 3.3V LDO (U20) and the FT231XS internal LDO, causing excessive current, instability, or damage.

parsed.summary: The design files contain three anomalies: the isolated CAN transceivers have their isolated grounds and supplies tied to the non-isolated GND and 5V rails, defeating isolation; the e-stop status LED D30 is wired between ESTOP_OUT and itself, so it can never light; and the FT231XS 3V3OUT pin is tied to the +3V3 rail, creating LDO contention.

But the body diode of Q1 still conducts from USBC_VBUS_IN to +5V. So USB can still power +5V through body diode, but with a diode drop. That might be intended to prevent reverse current? Actually LTC4412 CTL is used to force the MOSFET off. If CTL is high, the MOSFET is off, so only body diode conducts. That provides reverse current protection but higher drop. The note in spec says "USB diode doesn't work, I guess need ideal diode to handle more power? LTC4412 controller and p-ch mosfet. need reverse current protection mostly". So they want ideal diode for low drop and reverse protection. If CTL is tied to VBUS, then when USB is present, CTL is high, turning off the MOSFET, so it acts as a simple diode. That defeats the purpose of the ideal diode! Let's check LTC4412 datasheet: CTL pin: "Control Input. When CTL is high, the GATE pin is pulled high, turning off the external P-channel MOSFET. When CTL is low, the GATE pin is pulled low, turning on the MOSFET." So if CTL is tied to VIN (USB VBUS), then when USB is present, CTL is high, MOSFET is off. So the ideal diode is disabled. But the body diode of Q1 still conducts from USBC_VBUS_IN to +5V. So USB can still power +5V through body diode, but with a diode drop. That might be intended to prevent reverse current? Actually LTC4412 CTL is used to force the MOSFET off. If CTL is high, the MOSFET is off, so only body diode conducts. That provides reverse current protection but higher drop. The note in spec says "USB diode doesn't work, I guess need ideal diode to handle more power? LTC4412 controller and p-ch mosfet. need reverse current protection mostly". So they want ideal diode for low drop and reverse protection. If CTL is tied to VBUS, then when USB is present, CTL is high, turning off the MOSFET, so it acts as a simple diode. That defeats the purpose of the ideal diode! Let's check LTC4412 datasheet: CTL pin: "Control Input. When CTL is high, the GATE pin is pulled high, turning off the external P-channel MOSFET. But the body diode of Q1 still conducts from USBC_VBUS_IN to +5V. So USB can still power +5V through body diode, but with a diode drop. That might be intended to prevent reverse current? Actually LTC4412 CTL is used to force the MOSFET off. If CTL is high, the MOSFET is off, so only body diode conducts. That provides reverse current protection but higher drop. The note in spec says "USB diode doesn't work, I guess need ideal diode to handle more power? LTC4412 controller and p-ch mosfet. need reverse current protection mostly". So they want ideal diode for low drop and reverse protection. If CTL is tied to VBUS, then when USB is present, CTL is high, turning off the MOSFET, so it acts as a simple diode. That defeats the purpose of the ideal diode! Let's check LTC4412 datasheet: CTL pin: "Control Input. When CTL is high, the GATE pin is pulled high, turning off the external P-channel MOSFET.
